Intercession
in-ter-sesh´un
n. (a pleading with God on behalf of another; Christ's unfinished priestly work, and the Spirit's inarticulate help, and the church's duty)
Latin intercessio, a going between, from intercedere (inter- between + cedere to go). The high priest went between God and the people with blood. Christ now goes between with His own.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Intercession is a going between: prayer or pleading offered to God for another. The church is commanded to it: “I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men” (1Ti 2:1). But the load-bearing Intercessor is not the church. It is the risen Christ: “Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them” (Heb 7:25). Paul locates that work at the Father's right hand: “who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us” (Rom 8:34). The Spirit does a different and inward work of the same name: “the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered” (Rom 8:26). And Isaiah had already put the vocation on the Servant: “he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isa 53:12). Christ's intercession is not a second sacrifice. It is the once-offered Priest presenting the finished work, always, for those who come unto God by Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines intercession as the act of interceding; mediation; interposition between parties at variance, with a view to reconciliation; prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another.

expand to see more

INTERCES'SION, n. [L. intercessio, from intercedo. See Intercede.]

The act of interceding; mediation; interposition between parties at variance, with a view to reconciliation;

prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another, sometimes against another.

He bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors. Isaiah 53:12.

Key Scripture

Heb 7:25 — "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."

Rom 8:34 — "Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us."

Rom 8:26 — "Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered."

1Ti 2:1 — "I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men;"

Isa 53:12 — "Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors."

Modern Corruption

Christ's intercession is either forgotten, as if the cross were the whole priesthood, or farmed out to saints and a queen of heaven.

expand to see more

Rome installed a court of secondary intercessors — Mary, the saints, a priesthood that still mediates as if Hebrews were unfinished. Hebrews 7:25 gives the office to the One who ever liveth, and it gives the reason He can save to the uttermost: that living intercession. A dead saint cannot occupy it. A queen of heaven is a rival to it. The church on earth is commanded to make intercessions; it is never invited to share the unique priesthood of the Son.

Protestant forgetfulness is quieter. The cross is preached as finished, which it is, and then Christ is spoken of as if He were done working. Romans 8:34 will not have it. The same Christ who died, who is risen, who is at the right hand, also maketh intercession for us. The session is not retirement. A people that never thinks of Christ praying for them will soon pray as if everything depended on the heat of their own words.

The Spirit's groanings are not a second gospel. They are help in infirmity, because we know not what we should pray for as we ought. That is comfort for the inarticulate, not a license for uninterpreted utterance as a mark of standing. The Intercessor in heaven speaks clearly. The Spirit within translates our weakness. Neither replaces the Word.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek entygchanō (G1793), to fall in with, plead; enteuxis (G1783), intercession; Hebrew paga (H6293), to meet, make intercession.

expand to see more

Greek entygchanō (G1793) — to intercede; Hebrews 7:25, Romans 8:27, 8:34.

Greek enteuxis (G1783) — intercession; 1 Timothy 2:1, 4:5.

Hebrew paga (H6293) — to meet, lay upon, intercede; Isaiah 53:12, made intercession for the transgressors.

Usage

"“He ever liveth to make intercession” — the priesthood is not a past event."

"“Who also maketh intercession for us” — said of the Christ who died and is risen."

"“Intercessions... be made for all men” — the church's duty, not a rival priesthood."
